opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the hardest questions in running a research team, and honestly I don't think anyone has fully solved it.

The traditional metrics, like paper counts, citations, or how many top-conference acceptances you have, are easy to measure, but they can push people in the wrong direction. If you optimize for papers, you get a lot of incremental work: small tweaks, slightly better numbers on a benchmark, something that's publishable within six months. That's not where the real breakthroughs come from, especially in a field like robotics, where some of the most important problems take years before they produce anything that looks like a clean result.

So what I care about more is impact, and I try to define it broadly. Did your work change how other people think about a problem? Did it become something the team or the community builds on? Did it actually make a robot do something it couldn't do before, in the real world and not just in a demo video? Sometimes the most valuable contribution is infrastructure: a simulator, a data pipeline, a training framework. It may never become a famous paper, but it enables ten other projects. If your evaluation system doesn't reward that, people stop doing it, and the whole team slows down.

The second thing is that you have to evaluate over the right time horizon. Research is high-variance by nature. If you judge people every quarter, you're effectively telling them not to take risks. I'd rather see someone attempt something ambitious and fail in an informative way than succeed at something safe. A good evaluation should look at the quality of the bet: was the question important, was the approach well reasoned, and did we learn something even if it didn't work?

Third, I think taste matters a lot, and it's underrated. Choosing the right problem at the right time is probably the most important skill a researcher has. That's hard to quantify, but over a few years you can see it. Some people consistently pick problems that turn out to matter, and that's something you can recognize and reward.

Finally, in the current era, a lot of progress comes from large teams working together on big systems, not from individuals writing single-author papers. So evaluation also has to account for collaboration: whether someone makes the people around them more effective. Fitting this into individual performance reviews is genuinely difficult, but if you ignore it, you end up with a group of very smart people all optimizing for their own line on the CV, and that's not how you build something like a general-purpose robot.

So, in short: less counting, more judgment, a longer time horizon, and real rewards for the unglamorous work that moves the whole field forward.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts publication metrics with broader impact, including real-world robot capabilities, but does not identify incorporation into products as a distinct performance dimension.

r002.rationale: The response describes evaluating impact, time horizon, research judgment, and collaboration together as parts of performance evaluation.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, because I've sat on both sides of it, being evaluated and evaluating others.

My honest view is that the metrics we lean on most heavily, paper count, citation count, h-index, are convenient precisely because they're easy, not because they're right. They measure activity and visibility. They don't measure whether you actually moved the field. And once people know the metric, they optimize for it. You end up with incremental papers that are safe to publish rather than ideas that might fail.

What I'd rather ask is: what did this person figure out that nobody knew before? Can you name one or two things they did that changed how others work? For a strong researcher, that answer usually comes quickly. If you have to dig through a CV to find it, that tells you something.

The second thing I care about is the trajectory of their taste. Did they pick problems that mattered, or problems that were available? Choosing the right problem is most of the game, and it's the hardest thing to teach.

The third is honesty and reproducibility. In robotics especially, a demo video can hide a lot. I'd rather see someone with fewer results that hold up than many that quietly don't.

And finally, I think time horizon matters. Evaluating people every year pushes everyone toward short-term wins. Good research often looks like nothing is happening for a while. If you want people to take real risks, you have to give them room to fail for a few years without penalty. That's uncomfortable for institutions, but I think it's the price of doing anything genuinely new.

r001.rationale: The response critiques paper counts and citations and discusses research influence, but does not distinguish publication impact from impact through incorporation into products.

r002.rationale: The response presents several factors for evaluating performance, including discoveries, problem choice, reproducibility, and time horizon.

astra-6.text:
I think researchers should be evaluated primarily on the quality and impact of their work, rather than simply on the number of papers they publish. Are they asking important questions? Are they producing reliable results? Does their work help other people make progress?

The time horizon matters, too. If we evaluate everyone only on what they deliver each year, we encourage safe, incremental projects. Research needs room for ambitious ideas that might take several years—and might fail. So I would look at both the contributions someone has made and the judgment and rigor they bring to pursuing difficult problems. Mentoring and collaboration should count as well, because a researcher’s contribution often extends beyond their own publications.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts work quality and impact with paper counts, but does not distinguish publication based impact from incorporation into products.

r002.rationale: It lists several considerations for performance, but does not state that multiple dimensions of impact are considered together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think researchers should be evaluated by the quality and impact of their work over a longer period, rather than simply by how many papers they publish. Did they identify an important problem? Did they contribute a new idea or help us understand something better? And can other people build on what they did?

There’s also a question of risk. If every project has to produce a positive result quickly, people will naturally choose safer problems. Good research sometimes means spending a long time on an idea that doesn’t work. We should look at the judgment behind those choices and what was learned, as well as the final outcome. Publications matter, but they’re only part of the picture.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts paper count with the quality and impact of research, but does not identify incorporation into products as a separate performance dimension.

r002.rationale: It says evaluation should consider quality, impact, research choices, what was learned, and final outcomes together, with publications only part of the picture.
